facts.claim: Duolingo uses a freemium model, keeping learning free while monetizing through paid subscriptions.
facts.excerpt: The freemium business model is good for our mission and our business. Duolingo started as a free product, and we remain committed to offering free learning for all while monetizing through a valuable paid experience.

facts.claim: Duolingo reported 52.7M daily active users, 133.1M monthly active users, and 12.2M paid subscribers as of Q4 2025.
facts.excerpt: As of Q4 2025, we have 52.7M DAUs, 133.1M MAUs, and 12.2M paid subscribers.

facts.claim: Duolingo says its growth investment is mostly in product R&D, with marketing used strategically to accelerate growth.
facts.excerpt: our investment in growth is almost all in product R&D, with marketing used to strategically accelerate growth.

strategy.observation: Duolingo describes its product as built on play, using gamification and design to make learning fun.
strategy.offer_link: Voice actors and audio production could help keep language lessons lively and consistent with that playful product experience, especially if the team is producing a lot of short-form learning content that needs to feel polished and engaging.
hypotheses: The learning content team may be looking for ways to improve learner engagement through audio.
Duolingo may need scalable voice and audio workflows across many languages, lessons, or content updates.
The team may value faster turnaround on new lesson content without sacrificing audio quality.
strategy.angle: Duolingo’s learning experience is built around play, so audio quality is likely doing more than just reading prompts aloud.
strategy.fit_reason: Duolingo’s language-learning format makes voice and audio a plausible contributor to lesson quality and engagement, and the company explicitly emphasizes fun, game-like product design, which aligns with polished audio production.

draft.subject: Audio for lesson content
draft.body:
Duolingo’s learning experience is built around play, so audio is doing more than reading prompts aloud.

I provide voice actors and audio production for language-learning content. That tends to matter when lesson audio has to stay lively, clear, and consistent across frequent updates.

If your team is producing a lot of short-form lesson content, are you handling voice casting and audio in-house, or do you bring it out when volume picks up?
